records.content:
Agent of change

An individual, group, or organisation capable of exercising agency to influence the direction of change. Agency refers to the ability of an actor to become relevant within a particular context and to shape actions.
Source: Leipold & Winkel (2017); Simoens et al. (2022).

Sustainable transitions

Processes of changing unsustainable systems and practices
towards more sustainable ways of living.
See also 

Societal transformation.

Societal transformation

Fundamental changes in social structures, institutions,
behaviours, and relationships.
Related concept: 

Sustainable transitions.

1. How can you use and contribute to this Workbook?

records.content:
Initiated as a joint effort by TU Berlin, Politecnico di Milano and TU Delft within the ENHANCE Alliance of European Universities of Technology, the City as Laboratory Workbook is an open-access resource designed to support the reflective practice of critically examining one’s experiences, intended actions and assumptions to strengthen transdisciplinary learning as a way to develop knowledge from, for and with society. As such, the Workbook encourages citizens including students, educators, practitioners, policymakers and community members to collectively address interconnected social, economic, and environmental challenges.

This preliminary version presents the first two modules, while the complete edition will include six modules in total, accompanied by a glossary, dedicated worksheets for hands-on exercises compiled into a Learning Journey Portfolio and the reference list covering all modules. Each module combines theoretical insights with practical exercises, audiovisual explainers, and cases and tools from various sources. Cases present real-life examples of collaboration, while tools offer transferable learning activities aligned with specific objectives. Together, the modules create opportunities to connect, explore ideas, reflect and exchange learning experiences.

By integrating diverse perspectives and knowledge types, the Workbook strengthens learners’ ability to navigate complexity and supports the co-creation of sustainable practices across disciplines, sectors and cultural contexts.

records.content:
Explain the motivation, structure, expected use, contributions to and benefits from this Workbook.

Define key concepts such as change, transition, transformation and sustainability mean to you.

Develop  the willingness to apply the Workbook content to your personal development by starting to compile a Learning Journey Portfolio.

An invitation to share knowledge, collaborate and learn from each other to achieve societal goals. The motivation behind



Figure 1:Gap between the imaginary of the “City as a Laboratory” and current situation. Visual by Ariele Empirio.

As a citizen of this world, whether affiliated with an academic, government, business, cultural or civil society organisation, you may see yourself in 

Figure 1, perhaps curious about your role as an 

agent of change: someone able to move from the current situation to a desired one (Simoens et al 2022↗).  In this role, you may be concerned with “sustainability or survivability challenges”.

At one extreme, people with basic comfort and liveability face sustainability challenges, understood as interconnected social, economic, and environmental issues that affect long-term well-being. On the other extreme, those experiencing multiple scarcities (e.g., housing, food, energy, and water) struggle with survival due to limited access to resources. While in some societies the differences between these extremes are greater, both groups can be found worldwide, contributing to environmental degradation for different reasons: the former through overconsumption and waste, and the latter through a lack of technological and economic means to use resources sustainably ( Halawa, 2024↗ ). As a result, each group experiences the consequences of challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, migration, urbanisation, and threats to sustainability and democracy in different ways, depending on their circumstances. In this context, one can understand “democracy” (†see glossary) as the meaningful participation of citizens in decision-making, which also implies that responsible citizens actively engage in shaping acceptable standards and inclusive futures for all, regardless of group affiliation ( Ribeiro et al, 2025↗ ). Although values like sustainability and democracy are often framed as universal or long-term goals, this can lead to one group imposing them on others, overlooking cultural differences and failing to acknowledge their own limitations in addressing complex challenges. Accordingly, interventions should not be transferred uncritically between contexts; they require adaptable and flexible design that accounts for evolving values and needs over time ( Davis & Nathan et al 2015↗ ).

Sustainable transitions

Similarly, in the places where you live, study or work, you may observe or personally experience somehow unequal access to basic living standards within and across neighbourhoods and social groups. You may have noticed that tensions between shared and private resources often amplify inequalities and lead to conflicts between identities and competing visions of the future. This awareness may motivate you to imagine more equitable, ethical, and responsible ways of thinking and acting, both individually and collectively. At the same time, you may wonder whether it is possible or worthwhile to address today’s complex challenges without sufficient resources or a clear role in decision-making within your community or organisation. You may also simply not know where to begin or how to make a meaningful difference.

These reflections may lead to a broader question about your own role in addressing such challenges. Hence, do you see yourself as a change- or transition-maker? Keep in mind that “change”  (†see glossary) is not only the result of moving from one situation to another which may not always be desired. Change is also an ongoing process that unfolds across different spatial and temporal scales, with or without your involvement ( Mierlo & Beer, 2020↗ ).

When referring to change toward a desired state of sustainability, and to avoid labeling societies as developed or underdeveloped, the term “sustainable development” (†see glossary) has gradually been replaced by “sustainable transitions” (†see glossary) or “transformations”, although these terms do not carry the same meaning. To begin with, a “societal transition” refers to large-scale changes in how society thinks and acts. These transitions can result from abrupt events that disrupt the status quo, prompting groups to respond with solidarity and reinforce existing identities. They may take time to unfold as practices change and identities are reshaped ( Janssen et al., 2022↗ ). To become “sustainable”, transitions should be inclusive or representative to all societal groups . In the process, one must admit that “sustainable transformations” (†see glossary) are transformative visions of the future shaped by whose perspectives and comfort levels define the challenge, as well as by the identities, values and positions of those involved ( Halawa, 2024↗ ). As illustrated in the podcast suggested for the practical exercise of this module ( see below Task 1.2. what does sustainability mean to you? ), researchers from various fields discuss how actions considered sustainable in one place may worsen conditions for other groups of the (world’s) population.

Given this complexity and plurality of perspectives, engaging in societal transitions and transformations whether sustainable or not requires continuous learning and reflection. Therefore, this Workbook is intended to support you in designing the change you seek in your own life. In doing so, you can rethink your role and responsibilities as a transition-maker through a learning journey that encourages you to explore complex challenges and experiment with new ways of thinking and acting, both individually and collectively.  To support your learning, we invite you to revisit your personal development plan and compile your work and experiences from the Workbook modules you follow in your own context into a “Learning Journey Portfolio” (†see glossary).

This Workbook further encourages you to go through this journey with a cooperative, and hopeful yet critical attitude:

Lasting change takes time. It often begins with you, but it is not only about you. Take time to understand the challenges, imagine ways to address them, and view tensions and conflicts as opportunities to learn and adapt. Exchange perspectives with others along the way.

Start small but act with purpose. Choose wisely when to act about these challenges and when not to, based on your role and resources. Acting includes both small steps, like building connections, but also refraining from action or even doing nothing for now. Transformation efforts also require caring for yourself and your loved ones, so you are ready to act when it matters most.

Every result holds a lesson. Reflect on your learning journey, including both process and results for yourself, others, society, and the environment. Consider feedback (e.g. reactions, ideas, beliefs) to support your well-being and personal growth.

records.content: Cities are key centres of human activity, creativity, and knowledge and major contributors to interconnected social, economic, and environmental challenges. At the same time, they bring diverse people together, making them places to collaborate and explore alternative ways of thinking and acting. Do you perceive your city, village or community or the spot where you work, learn and live as a space to change everyday practices, live as yourself with others, and develop sustainable ways of living? This module elaborates on the City as a Laboratory and guides you through seven tasks to help revisiting and sharing how did you connect and define with a real-life example of a challenge that as a basis for developing and refining your learning journey as illustrated through an individual portfolio, parts of which you will share with others.

records.content:
Explain the “City as a Laboratory” idea as a shared space for experimentation and developing knowledge.

Define the boundaries of the chosen real-life example.

Identify the role of cross-boundary collaborations in supporting societal transitions.

Describe the main steps and strategy for change, transformation and learning.

Reflect on personal motivations, roles, and capabilities for acting as an agent of change.

Figure 1:Gap between the imaginary of the “City as a Laboratory” and current situation. Visual by Ariele Empirio.

By following the metaphor of the “City as a Laboratory”, this Workbook invites you to see cities not simply as places that grow “on their own.” Instead, this module encourages you to imagine cities as shared places and projects where everyone, not just a few, can take part, make their own choices, and influence what happens by sharing their ideas, hopes, and skills 

Saunders, 2010

Philipp & Jende, 2025.

In the imagined view shown in 

Figure 1, the term “city” is not about size or location, but about places where people try to live their own lives together with others in fair and supportive conditions while learning from one another 

Philipp & Jende, 2025. In this imaginary, being part of a place means more than simply living there. It means being part of a community.

Research on pre-industrial understandings of dwelling suggests that the French term habiter and the English notion of dwelling imply more than simply residing in a place. They point to an active social life within a community and an ongoing relationship with one’s environment. People shape places, and places shape people 

Henri & Donald, 1991.

However, consumer lifestyles and entertainment industries have often transformed cities into spaces centred on commercialised public areas and high levels of consumption 

Wilson & Erk, 2023. While this development has supported economic growth, it also contributes to excessive resource use, emissions, and waste, while affecting well-being through stress, overwork, inactivity, individualism, and social isolation 

Kronenberg et al., 2024.

records.content:
By Francesco Vergani, Valentina Faccoetti & Juliette-Cortes-Arevalo

Choose a real-life challenge among the clusters listed below to uncover how your personal experience shapes your connection with it.

15 minutes own story

15 minutes to interview other actors

Use the questions below to explore your connection to the challenge and whom would you like to support in addressing it. If you wish, use the same questions to ask people who are interested in or affected by the challenge about their experience to enrich your perspective with their insights.

A space to take notes and reflect

Reflective storytelling, Challenge-based inquiry, Reconstruct & Intervene.

This exercise builds on your current understanding of the challenge. Other perspectives may not yet be visible and can be explored further by using the same questions to interview other actors.

Use the guiding questions of one challenge cluster to explore it in relation with your work or interests

Shared spaces and collective practices

Who creates and governs these in the future?

Shared spaces are increasingly shaped by tensions between shared resources and privatisation.

Questions to explore

How can new shared spaces be created?

What forms of governance can involve citizens?

Justice and care

Who has access to wellbeing?

Access to health, green space, mobility and safety varies.

Questions to explore

How can territorial inequalities be reduced?

How can overlooked needs become visible?

Vulnerability and climate adaptation:

How can we live with a changing climate?

Places, in for example, cities will face increasing exposure to extreme weather events, resource scarcity and biodiversity loss. Adaptation is not only a technical challenge but also requires new ways of inhabiting and relating to an environment.

Questions to explore

How can one respond to extreme weather and new forms of vulnerability or exposure to harm or risk?

How can disrupted ecological relationships be restored?

How can natural and built systems be better integrated?

How can territories address the challenge without increasing inequalities?

Memory and conflict:

Whose stories shape  transformation?

Regeneration is the process of improving and transforming parts of a place to make them stable locations to live and work. However, it often creates tensions between memories, identities, interests, and different visions of the future, where some stories are highlighted while others are overlooked or erased.

Questions to explore

How can marginalised histories be recognised and valued?

How can conflicts between long-term residents and newcomers be addressed?

How can development avoid pushing aside people’s culture or stories?

How can conflict support transformation?

The right to transform:

Who has the power to shape the future of a place?

Urban transformation is often driven by a limited number of government and economic actors. Yet emerging forms of participation, activism and civic engagement are reshaping who has the power to envision, influence, and shape the future of cities.

Questions to explore

Who is excluded from decisions about the future of a place?

How can participation be broadened and made more meaningful?

Which non-human actors should have a voice in decision-making?

What new forms of democracy could emerge?

Start with your personal connection. Describe a moment where you noticed the challenge. Be specific (e.g. “on my daily commute…” or “in my neighbourhood…”).

Describe why it matters? Explain why this problem is important to you and what consequences does it have for whom.

What does it bother you about this situation? Share what feels wrong, unfair, or unsustainable.

What inspires you to act? Consider also what triggered your interest, positively.

Who is mostly affected by this situation? Mention people, groups, or even the environment affected by this problem situation.

What do you wish it could be different? Share your feelings and observations about the change you wish to see and why is not happening yet.

What photos or visual helps to illustrate the situation? Acknowledge the source and copyrights as necessary.

To conclude, formulate a problem statement following the below guidance: "How can [choose an actor who has key resources or responsibilities to take action on the challenge right now and you wish to support] address [define the chosen actor’s main objective] without [define the main two unintended consequences this actor wants to avoid]

Creating places where people and other living beings can thrive together.

By Francesco Vergani & Valentina Facoetti

Under preparation

Add caption

Cities and everyday environments are often imagined and designed as spaces made by and for humans. Yet they are continuously inhabited, shaped and transformed by plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and other non-human agents. This module introduces More-than-Human and Multispecies Design as approaches for moving beyond Human-Centred approach and reconsidering Design as a relational practice within interconnected ecological worlds. Learners will explore how anthropocentric assumptions shape urban environments and how non-human agency can be acknowledged in city design. Attention is given to living and non-living agents, whose behaviours, needs and capacities are frequently overlooked despite their central role in urban ecosystems. Through data collection, relationship mapping, reversed perspective approach and future envisioning, learners will identify non-human agents, investigate the relations and stressors that shape its everyday conditions and reflect on existing power dynamics. They will therefore transform the insights gathered into a speculative future scenario “beyond the human”, aimed at fostering a mutually beneficial coexistence between the human and non-human worlds. The module encourages participants to document a contextualised multispecies relationship, to critically question anthropocentric assumptions and to propose an possible intervention that is attentive to coexistence, care, temporality and the autonomy of different forms of life.

Recognise the limits of designing only for humans and why it matters to consider other living beings in the design of shared spaces.

Learn to see a place from the perspective of the plants and animals that live there.

Imagine Imagine a future that supports coexistence between humans and nature.
